source.title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model

accepted.question_text: Do the observed redshifts of galaxies and quasars necessarily imply that the universe is expanding, or can a physically and observationally supported non-cosmological redshift mechanism, such as gravitational redshift, tired light, variable mass, chronometric cosmology, or multiple scattering, explain those redshifts without producing unacceptable image blurring, frequency dependence, or conflicts with intergalactic-medium constraints?

evidence.quote: Some observations will be discussed or rediscussed in order to show that these facts were not strictly proven. The possibility of alternative hypotheses different from the Big Bang theory is still open.

All these proposed mechanisms show us that it is quite possible to construct a scenario with non-cosmological redshifts. Nonetheless, all these theories are at present just speculations without direct experimental or observational support.

accepted.question_text: Can the Tolman surface-brightness test provide a decisive observational distinction between an expanding universe and a non-expanding universe when the observed surface-brightness dependence on redshift must be disentangled from galaxy luminosity evolution, intergalactic absorption by metals or dust, and possible methodological errors?

evidence.quote: Expansion model predicts a (1 + z)−4 dependence, and must therefore invoke special ad hoc evolution to close the gap between theory and observations. This makes the Tolman test useless since we cannot separate its results from the evolution of galaxies.

We do not know how large it is but we must bear in mind that before we know it, we will not be able to contrast the different cosmological hypotheses. Errors due to inaccuracies of the method are also possible.

accepted.question_text: If Type Ia supernova light curves show the expected cosmological time dilation by roughly a factor of 1 + z, why do quasars apparently lack the same time-dilation effect at their cosmological redshifts, and can any non-expansion cosmology reproduce the supernova time-dilation signal without contradicting quasar and gamma-ray-burst timing observations?

evidence.quote: These results seem to be in contradiction with the results for QSOs[61], which do not present time dilation as would be expected if they were at the distance corresponding to the cosmological redshift. If this analysis is correct, either the redshift of the QSOs is not cosmological (see §2.3.1) or these do not present the expected effect of the expansion.

Anyway, supernovae results are, in my opinion, the most impressive and solid test about the reality of the expansion, and it might only be rejected if some alternative theory can emulate the time dilation too.

accepted.question_text: Do absorption-line measurements in high-redshift clouds demonstrate that the cosmic microwave background radiation temperature increases with redshift as T proportional to 1 + z, or are those inferred temperatures too dependent on collisional excitation, ultraviolet pumping, infrared dust emission, and other local excitation mechanisms to serve as a definitive test?

evidence.quote: Therefore, previous works have not proven the increase of CMBR temperature with z by a factor (1 + z).
The result depends on the estimate of other contributions to the excitation, so nothing can yet be concluded definitively from this test.

accepted.question_text: Can apparent-magnitude-versus-distance and angular-size-versus-redshift observations distinguish static and expanding cosmologies when the analysis depends on uncertain luminosity evolution and on identifying standard candles or standard rods whose intrinsic size, mass, and brightness do not vary with redshift except according to a known evolutionary scheme?

evidence.quote: This disagreement could however be solved by an increase of luminosity at higher redshift due to the evolution of galaxies (which is a possible observational result pointed out from deep infrared FIRES and HST data[72]), so the uncertainties in the luminosity evolution do not allow this to be a proof against expansion.

However, the main problem of such a type of test is the identification of the “standard stick” for which one knows reliably its non-variation with redshift, or its variation with a well-known evolutionary scheme so we must be cautious too to interpret the results of this test as a definitive proof of a particular cosmological model, in this case the static Universe.

accepted.question_text: Does the temperature of the intergalactic medium, as inferred from the small-scale falloff of the Lyman-alpha forest power spectrum, evolve with redshift as expected from adiabatic cooling in an expanding universe, or is the reported absence of redshift evolution evidence that requires another explanation?

evidence.quote: It is typically inferred to be 20000 K, but there is no evidence of evolution with redshift[80]. Yet in the Big Bang, that temperature ought to adiabatically decrease as space expands everywhere.

If these measurements are confirmed by other means, it could be another indicator that the universe is not really expanding unless other explanations arise. At present it is early to establish definitively this claim.

accepted.question_text: When galaxies or compact galaxy groups appear connected by filaments, radio material, emission structures, or positional alignments but have strongly discordant redshifts, are those systems chance projections along the line of sight, or do they indicate physical associations in which at least some galaxy redshifts are non-cosmological?

evidence.quote: There are some cases in which “apparently” connected or interacting galaxies have different redshifts[81, 26, 82]. One of the most famous cases is Stephan’s quintet(SQ)[83].

There is also a Hα-filament which is extending throughout NGC 7320 with velocity at 6500 km/s instead of 800 km/s expected for this galaxy[86], which is somewhat unlikely to be there by chance. The conclusions about SQ are not clear yet.

Example: the Seyfert 1 galaxy NGC 7603 (z = 0.029) appears connected to a companion galaxy (z = 0.056) and along the thin filament there are two further HII-galaxies with redshifts 0.24 and 0.39[92, 93], which makes the system much more unprobable in terms of cosmological redshifts.

accepted.question_text: Are high-redshift quasars, or quasi-stellar objects, physically associated with and possibly ejected from nearby low-redshift active galaxies, with intrinsic or quantized redshift components, rather than lying at the large cosmological distances implied by their observed redshifts?

evidence.quote: Non-orthodox hypothesis shared by very few astronomers (Arp, Burbidge & Burbidge and few others) claim that QSOs are being ejected by low redshift active galaxies.
The main idea in any case is that QSOs are really at the same distance than nearby galaxies in spite of their high redshifts.
Detailed investigations of several QSO-galaxy pairs show that the galaxy and QSO are apparently connected.

accepted.question_text: If quasar redshifts measure cosmological distance, why should quasars evolve so that their average apparent brightness remains comparable across very different redshifts, while their number density peaks near redshift 2.5 to 3 and then declines at both lower and higher redshifts, instead of increasing naturally toward the earliest epochs as expected for galaxy seeds?

evidence.quote: Why QSOs should evolve in just this way to produce this coincidence of apparent magnitudes whatever it is its redshift?[127].

The standard model predicts that QSOs, the seeds of all galaxies, should be more numerous at earliest epochs, so apparently there is a problem here, which might be solved ad hoc, but not as a natural prediction of the model.

accepted.question_text: What physically coherent model of quasars at cosmological distances can jointly explain their required luminosities in compact variable regions, apparently superluminal radio motions, lack of expected time dilation, Faraday-rotation behavior with redshift, high metallicity and dust content at high redshift, and the failure or uniformity problems of damped Lyman-alpha absorber detections?

evidence.quote: Other anomalies or questions with not very clear answers have arisen about the nature of QSO and the suspicion that their distance is not as high as pointed out by the cosmological interpretation of their redshift.
Superluminal motions of distant sources (D) are observed, i.e. angular speeds ω between two radio emitting blobs which imply linear velocities v = Dω greater than the speed light[129].

The absorption lines of damped Lyα systems are seen in QSOs. The HST NICMOS spectrograph has searched to see these objects directly in the infrared, but failed for the most part to detect them[134]. Moreover, the relative abundances have surprising uniformity, unexplained in the standard model[135] and, as said (see §2.2), the temperature of these clouds does not change with redshift[80], a fact which does not fit the normal predictions of the standard model.

accepted.question_text: Is the cosmic microwave background radiation necessarily a relic of a high-energy primordial universe, or can an astrophysical or static-universe scenario explain its observed temperature, nearly blackbody spectrum, isotropy, and thermalization without requiring an opaque universe that conflicts with the observed transparency to high-redshift radio galaxies?

evidence.quote: Anyway, the radiation is there and the question is the origin of this radiation not the discoverer. Is the high energy primordial Universe the only possible scenario?
The mechanism of thermalization in any of these cases is perhaps the hardest problem.
At present there is not a satisfactory alternative scenario which has no problem to explain the Microwave Background Radiation, so the standard scenario seems the best solution.

accepted.question_text: How can observations of particles with energies above 60 × 10^18 electron-volts be reconciled with the standard interpretation of the cosmic microwave background radiation, given that interactions with microwave-background photons impose a theoretical propagation limit for particles traveling more than about 20 to 50 megaparsecs?

evidence.quote: For example, many particles are seen with energies over 60 × 1018 eV. But that is the theoretical energy limit for anything traveling for more than 20-50 Mpc because of interaction with microwave background photons[161]. This is a problem for the actual interpretation of CMBR in the Big Bang theory.

accepted.question_text: Do cosmic microwave background anisotropy measurements and acoustic-peak fits provide robust predictions of the standard cosmological model, or are the fitted peaks and inferred parameters vulnerable to ad hoc refitting, foreground contamination from Galactic dust or other sources, and alternative interpretations such as quasi-steady-state cosmology or modified Newtonian dynamics?

evidence.quote: Apparently, the history of Microwave Background Radiation is a set of predictions which do not fit the observations but allow to modify the model to fit them ad hoc. This is called “successful predictions of the standard model”.

Apparently, these remarks were unfruitful since all the corrections of the galactic contamination continue to be carried out in the same wrong way: using templates and/or constant spectral index of the galactic dust contamination.

Nonetheless, subsequent observations, like those of Boomerang balloon-borne[164], have proven that, at least in some regions of low Galactic contamination, the microwave background radiation anisotropies over a larger range of frequencies is frequency independent, so something which is not dust should be producing these anisotropies, probably the same source which emits the average CMBR.

accepted.question_text: Can primordial Big Bang nucleosynthesis be tested without circularly choosing inferred primordial abundances and adjustable parameters, and can it consistently account for low reported helium mass fractions, uncertain deuterium evolution and production mechanisms, excessive beryllium abundances, baryon-density requirements, and the preference in some fits for two rather than three neutrino species?

evidence.quote: However, galaxies of poor metal content, implying minimal stellar contamination, show the mass fraction of 4He as low as 0.21 [172]. Even allowing for error bars this is far too low to match the Big Bang predictions.
The Deuterium evolution and mechanisms of possible Deuterium production from the Big Bang until now are still not properly understood[174, 175].

Perhaps the most important aspect to criticize is the methodology itself to test the primordial nucleosynthesis[182]: Instead of trying to make predictions that can be tested by observation, cosmologists take observations that can be made, such as measurements of the abundances in Population II material, and try to determine the primordial abundances, knowing a priori what answer is needed to fit some particular model.
Still, as we see, some open questions are discussed in the model and whether this can be substituted by alternative models remains to be seen.

accepted.question_text: Is the universe sufficiently homogeneous and isotropic on large scales for the Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker assumptions used by standard cosmology, given reports of periodic galaxy walls, fractal-like inhomogeneities to at least 100–200 megaparsecs, a highly linear local Hubble law, large-scale streaming motions, and redshift periodicities in galaxies or quasars?

evidence.quote: The standard theory would require large-scale homogeneity on scales of distance larger than few tens of Mpc, and the distribution of galaxies and clusters of galaxies should be random on large scales.
However, other observations suggest the opposite conclusion: a striking linearity of the Hubble law in the distance range between 2 and 25 Mpc[203, 149]. This is the inhomogeneity paradox[4].

By itself, the fact that some observer sees isotropic background radiation is inconclusive: for this can be true in a static inhomogeneous universe, as well as in a spherically symmetric inhomogeneous universe where we are near a centre of symmetry[204]. So an open question is apparently present.
However, none of them can be understood in terms of the Cosmological Hypothesis.

accepted.question_text: Why does the observable universe appear to be dominated by matter rather than containing equal amounts of matter and antimatter, if protons do not decay and standard physics would otherwise produce matter and antimatter equally, and if experiments have not yet found successful evidence for the required asymmetry while antimatter galaxies would create unseen gamma-ray boundaries?

evidence.quote: Therefore, the Universe should be made up equally of matter and antimatter according to the standard model. Matter dominates the present universe apparently because of some form of asymmetry, such as CP violation asymmetry, that caused most anti-matter to annihilate with matter, but left much matter. Experiments are searching for evidence of this asymmetry, so far without success.
Other galaxies cannot be antimatter because that would create a matter-antimatter boundary with the intergalactic medium that would create gamma rays, which are not seen[217]. Another open question.

accepted.question_text: Where is the missing baryonic matter predicted by Big Bang baryon-density estimates, what is the nature and amount of any non-baryonic dark matter needed for Ωm around 0.3, and do galactic dark-matter haloes with the density profiles and satellite populations predicted by cold-dark-matter models actually exist on galactic scales?

evidence.quote: Stellar and cold gas in galaxies sum a baryonic matter 8+4−5% of the total amount of the Big Bang baryonic matter predictions[218], where is the rest of the baryonic material? From here stems another open question.
Which is the nature of the putative non-baryonic dark matter to achieve the current value of Ωm ≈ 0.3?

Some authors have been led to question the very existence of this dark matter on galactic scales since its evidence is weak[221, 223, 224, 225] and the predictions do not fit the observations: the halos are not cusped as predicted, the predicted angular momentum is much less than the observed one, the number of satellites around the galaxies is much less than the predictions, etc.

There is some dark matter, it is clear, but how much, and what is its nature? The success of the standard model to convert a hypothesis into a solid theory depends strongly on the answer to these open questions.

accepted.question_text: Is a positive cosmological constant or dark-energy density around ΩΛ ≈ 0.7 genuinely established by observations, or could the inference be shaped by prior model expectations, supernova dimming from intergalactic dust, metallicity dependence, host-galaxy extinction, alternative cosmological fits, and the enormous mismatch between observed Λ and quantum-field-theory vacuum-energy predictions?

evidence.quote: A genial prediction or a prejudice which conditions the actual measures? Another open question.

Type Ia Supernovae have also possibly a metallicity dependence and this would imply that the evidence for a non-zero cosmological constant from the SNIa Hubble Diagram may be subject to corrections for metallicity which are as big as the effects of cosmology[238].

Still some recent tests point out that other values are available in the literature. For instance, from the test angular size vs. redshift for ultracompact radio sources, it is obtained that Λ has the opposite sign[242].

Moreover, the actual values of ΩΛ have some consistency problem in the standard scenario of inflationary Big Bang. The cosmological constant predicted by the quantum field theory is a value much larger than those derived from observational cosmology.

accepted.question_text: How can standard cosmological galaxy evolution explain high-redshift quasars and galaxies that appear to have solar or supersolar metallicities, high dust content, little evolution in some line ratios from redshift 0 to 6.5, unexpectedly early massive hydrogen or galaxy structures, and mutually inconsistent reionization redshift estimates from Gunn-Peterson troughs, high-redshift galaxies, and WMAP cosmic-microwave-background anisotropies?

evidence.quote: But the latest evidence shows the existence of even higher than solar metallicities in the “earliest” QSOs and galaxies[55, 246, 247].
The amount of dust in high redshift galaxies and QSOs is also much higher than expected[253].
However, it is not enough with such a surprising claim, it needs to be demonstrated, and I do not see any evidence in favour of such a quick evolution in the local galaxies.
If we were going to believe that CMBR anisotropies are being correctly interpreted in terms of the standard cosmology, we would have again a new inconsistency.

accepted.question_text: Do the oldest Galactic stars truly have ages of 16–19 billion years or more, exceeding the standard cosmological age estimate of about 13.7 billion years, or are the stellar and cosmological age measurements still too inaccurate to establish a real conflict?

evidence.quote: Controversy also surrounds the age of the Universe. Cosmologists say the Universe is 8 to 15 billion years old, 13.7 Gyr according to the recent measures of WMAP[240], while stellar astronomers claim that the oldest stars in the Galaxy are as high 16 to 19 billion years old[259] or even older.
At present we have no firm proof for the age of the stars larger than the predicted age of the Universe by the standard model.
